items.title: Apache HTTP Server 2.4 vulnerabilities fixed by 2.4.71
items.summary: Classification: Critical, Solution: Official Fix, Exploit Maturity: Not Defined, CVSSv3.1: None, CVEs: CVE-2026-119618, CVE-2026-106023, CVE-2026-109163, Summary: CVE-2026-119618 (critical): mod_http2: heap corruption and RCE in assign_headers ¶ Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization vulnerability in Apache HTTP Server's mod_http2 in assign_headers() can lead to RCE. This issue affects Apache HTTP Server: from 2.4.55 through 2.4.70. Affected releases of mod_h2 from GitHub: from 2.0.8 through 2.0.42. CVE-2026-106023 (important): mod_md NULL pointer dereference leads to child process crash NULL pointer dereference vulnerability in Apache HTTP Server's mod_md during HTTP request processing. This issue affects Apache HTTP Server: from 2.4.30 through 2.4.70. CVE-2026-109163 (low): mod_vhost_alias 1 byte stack buffer overwrite (after CVE-2026-63292) ¶ Stack-based buffer overflow vulnerability in Apache HTTP Server's mod_vhost_alias (after CVE-2026-63292) This issue affects Apache HTTP Server: 2.4.69 and 2.4.70. See also: https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-119618, See also: https://www.wiz.io/blog/cve-2026-119618-rce-apache-http-server-vulnerability

Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization vulnerability in Apache HTTP Server's mod_http2 in assign_headers() can lead to RCE.

This issue affects Apache HTTP Server: 2.4.69 and 2.4.70. See also: https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-119618, See also: https://www.wiz.io/blog/cve-2026-119618-rce-apache-http-server-vulnerability

items.title: What 70 European CISOs told us about securing the AI era
items.summary: Last week I spent three days in Bavaria with more than 70 CISOs from across Europe, the Middle East and Africa at Leaders Point EMEA. Led by our CEO Nadav Zafrir and hosted with Team8’s CISO Village, it was our second Leaders Point and the first in Europe. We kept it invitation-only so people could speak openly. The timing was hard to miss. Over the past month, attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems have spoiled food and emptied shelves in stores across France and several other European countries. Nobody has yet been shown to be behind them. For anyone who still sees cyber risk as an IT problem, it was a sharp reminder of how physical it has become. As Nadav told the room, our industry is going through its most dramatic shift in 30 years. CISOs now have three jobs at once: protect their organizations from AI-driven threats, secure the AI their own teams use, and apply AI in their own defense. They are doing all of this while the rules are still being written. We host Leaders Point to listen, because Check Point’s strategy depends on seeing these challenges from our customers’ point of view. We covered a lot of ground, from a CISO panel on “Whose AI Can Europe Trust?” to national cyber leadership in the AI era and a look inside the frontier AI labs. Four themes kept coming back.

items.title: Australia may make knowingly selling unsafe AI a crime
items.summary: Australia’s government will consider creating a new criminal offense to punish AI companies which knowingly release harmful models. Canberra dangled that possibility yesterday when releasing the results of an investigation into OpenAI’s admission that its agents accessed non-public medical records – and that it didn’t disclose the incident for weeks. Security at the agency which held those records fell short of contemporary best practice but Canberra nonetheless ordered a rapid review into Australia’s ability to handle infosec incidents involving AI. That review landed yesterday, complete with 18 recommendations including one that would make it mandatory for AI companies to report misaligned behavior or security incidents involving their models, and perhaps impose criminal penalties for “egregious regulatory non-compliance.” Another recommendation calls for consideration of “A standalone ‘failure to prevent’ offence which would criminalize instances where the company is responsible for developing an AI model that engages in harmful conduct, and the company fails to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm.”

items.title: Britain, France set out first guidelines for commercial hacking firms
items.summary: Fourteen governments participating in the Pall Mall Process, a diplomatic effort led by Britain and France to rein in the global spyware industry, adopted their first guidelines for commercial hacking businesses on Wednesday. The French Foreign Ministry said the guidelines, aimed at addressing abuses associated with the proliferation of commercial cyber intrusion capabilities (CCICs), set out “the first global standard of responsible conduct.” “Access to certain capabilities once reserved for a handful of specialized government agencies has gradually widened: any actor can now buy ‘off the shelf’ the ability to silently penetrate a phone,” the ministry said. While it acknowledged those tools have been used in intelligence operations and to tackle organized crime, the ministry warned they “have also been implicated in surveillance campaigns targeting journalists, political officials, activists or businesses.” The guidelines are non-binding and endorsed by governments rather than industry organizations. They call on businesses that develop, sell or finance CCICs to vet their customers, establish technical safeguards against misuse and to maintain systems for monitoring and reporting abuses.

items.title: Ex-Hacker: Vibe-Coded APIs Riddled With Vulnerabilities
items.summary: Application programming interfaces are often a hackable road to the inside of a corporate network. And yet they're ubiquitous - with reason. Rather than run physical resources, developers can just call an API to spin up virtual servers, databases, artificial intelligence tools or other cloud-based resources on demand. Despite their starring role in many a hack, APIs are the IT "plumbing of our world today," said Alissa Knight, a self-described "recovering hacker," who was recruited by the U.S. intelligence community after being arrested. An API "plumbs our financial services and fintech. It plumbs our cars," she said. But increasingly, Knight told ISMG in an interview, APIs are getting less secure, not more. They are insecurely "vibe coded" by AI agents, rushed into production within days or even hours and not built in accordance with "shift left" or "secure by design" principles. Knight's demonstration of her technology at a Northern Virginia satellite cybersecurity conference last week showed a small swarm of AI agents finding, chaining and exploiting vulnerabilities in a synthetic environment she built to resemble a ground station, with an API modeled on one used to manage a satellite constellation.

items.title: ARTEX and AI-Powered Red Teaming Tools: What Defenders Need to Know
items.summary: A rapidly expanding ecosystem of AI-enabled tools such as ARTEX and CyberStrikeAI — marketed for red teaming and penetration testing — are being used by attackers to execute offensive operations autonomously. Their footprint is already substantial. Unit 42 has observed ARTEX used in intrusion attempts against multiple targets. Our Incident Response team investigated multiple intrusions in which the attacker’s server hosted an ARTEX console or used infrastructure and user agents associated with ARTEX. Separately, Unit 42 Managed Threat Hunting tracked a coordinated ARTEX campaign against customer cloud environments in sectors worldwide, including retail and consulting. External scrutiny has already disrupted project lifecycles: the author of ARTEX recently made the repository closed-source and ceased public development to prevent misuse. Emerging alternatives are rapidly filling the void, introducing new capabilities that threat actors will inevitably co-opt. items.title: Active ScreenConnect attacks breach MSPs, impact dozens of organizations
items.summary: ConnectWise is investigating an active malware campaign targeting managed service providers (MSPs) that uses compromised ScreenConnect environments to deploy rogue remote-access clients to customer devices. The campaign was first discovered Wednesday by cybersecurity firm Huntress, which says it has identified six compromised MSPs and 286 affected endpoints across 47 organizations, and that the number of victims continues to rise. "Our SOC is working an active campaign that started around 17:47 UTC today targeting cloud-hosted ScreenConnect instances," Huntress posted to Reddit. According to Huntress, attackers are using ScreenConnect's Run Command functionality to deploy ScreenConnect clients on managed endpoints, providing remote access outside of the legitimate MSP's ScreenConnect environment. The researchers also warned of a potentially more dangerous technique in which attackers can compromise an MSP technician's workstation when they initiate a ScreenConnect session with an infected customer device.

items.title: Critical RCE Vulnerability in Apache HTTP Server: Everything You Need To Know
items.summary: A critical synchronization vulnerability (CVE-2026-119618) has been identified in Apache HTTP Server’s HTTP/2 module (mod_http2). The flaw stems from a concurrent execution race condition within the assign_headers() function when handling shared resources. If successfully exploited, a remote, unauthenticated attacker can corrupt heap memory to achieve arbitrary code execution (RCE). As of the time of this blog’s publication, no exploit is available and there are no reports of exploitation in the wild. CVE-2026-119618 is a critical, high-severity vulnerability involving a race condition in the Apache HTTP Server, which was independently discovered by Anthropic and Google Cloud’s Vulnerability Research Team. Specifically, the flaw exists within the assign_headers() function of the HTTP/2 module (mod_http2). Due to improper synchronization when executing concurrent threads sharing resources, an attacker can trigger heap corruption. This memory corruption can ultimately be leveraged to achieve RCE on the hosting server, allowing unauthorized threat actors to execute arbitrary commands with the privileges of the web server process.

items.title: Maersk confirms data breach as WhiteArmor ransomware demands $5 million
items.summary: Shipping giant Maersk has confirmed that a threat actor breached systems belonging to a company it previously acquired and stole data. Ransomware group WhiteArmor claimed the attack over the weekend, threatening that it would release about 100GB of information allegedly exfiltrated from the company's logistics and supply-chain platform. The investigation into the incident is ongoing, but the shipping firm says that current evidence indicates that "no sensitive data has been disclosed." Maersk added that it does not expect disruptions to operations, and assures customers that they can continue booking and managing shipments through its systems as usual. “The incident is isolated to a local system, and we have found no indication that there has been any impact on other Maersk systems or customer and partner systems that connect to Maersk through integrations such as APIs and EDI,” Maersk states.

items.title: Analyysi: Tästä Stubb meitä varoitti
items.summary: Euroopassa on nähty runsaan viikon aikana poikkeuksellinen pommiuhkausten sarja. Ensin uhkaukset kohdistuivat matkustajakoneisiin, sitten tiedotusvälineisiin ja nyt tuhansiin kouluihin. Yli 300 koulua evakuoitiin Italiassa. Myös Skotlannissa ja Pohjois-Irlannissa satoihin kouluihin lähetettiin vastaavia viestejä, mutta viranomaiset arvioivat ne perättömiksi, eikä yhtä laajoihin evakuointeihin ryhdytty. Räjähteitä ei ole löytynyt. Silti uhkaukset ovat onnistuneet aiheuttamaan häiriöitä, pelkoa ja isoja kustannuksia. Juuri tämä lienee niiden tarkoitus. Perätön pommiuhkaus on halpa tapa saada aikaan kalliita seurauksia. Jos kyse on järjestelmällisestä hybridivaikuttamisesta, tekijä saavuttaa näin tavoitteensa ilman yhtäkään oikeaa pommia.
